spontaneous_understanding.central_story: Persistent annual deficits are the recurring explanation for France's debt buildup. Crisis-year jumps in 2009 and 2020 were never fully reversed, and borrowing continued between them. France collects more revenue than the EU average but spends even more above that average, particularly on cash benefits and public employees. Rising interest bills now add pressure without yet reaching historically exceptional GDP shares.
spontaneous_understanding.relationships: The story moves from accumulated debt to the recurring annual gap, then to the components of France's relative spending excess, and finally to the feedback from debt-service costs into that annual gap. It distinguishes a fiscal account of the buildup from a demonstrated market or political crisis.
what_changed_from_chart_reading: The prose names the global financial crisis and pandemic as coincident with the major jumps, confirming my date-based inference without claiming to isolate all mechanisms.
Definitions identify quarterly Maastricht debt and annual Eurostat accounts, including government coverage, revenue categories and the meaning of the balance.

The text and alt text clarify that historical chart-2 lines are France, Germany and EU27; Italy and Spain appear as latest-value comparisons. This resolves much of the ambiguity I had about peer trajectories, although visual identification alone remains weaker.
It adds that the EU27 also ran deficits throughout, so persistent borrowing alone is not uniquely French; the scale is the distinguishing claim.
It adds social protection's 2024 spending share and benefit indexation, providing some institutional context beyond the spending bars.
It explicitly notes the 2025 deficit improvement and attributes it to faster revenue growth, including new tax measures.
Source names, release dates, an alternative INSEE interest figure and a parser-review caveat fill in provenance absent from the chart images.
It explicitly says the accounts cannot decide whether there is a crisis, matching my main concern from stage1.

uncertainty_and_unanswered_questions: Why spending and revenue diverged historically remains unresolved; the prose acknowledges that the accounts do not identify the choices producing the gap.

The high-revenue comparison supports a relative fiscal description but does not by itself show that low taxes could never contribute to a deficit. Revenue includes more than taxes, as the prose itself explains.

The distinction between deficits and changes in the debt/GDP ratio remains implicit. GDP growth, inflation and other debt adjustments could matter, especially for the decline after 2020 despite deficits.
The mechanism behind the renewed interest increase is not explained: rates, refinancing and debt volume are not separated.
EU27-average weighting is still unspecified. 'Everything else' in the spending breakdown remains unexplained.
The title's borrowing claim is broader wording than the demonstrated negative annual budget balance; I understand it as shorthand for recurrent financing needs.
The prose presents recent numbers as released statistics and supplies release dates, but their provisional or revision status is not explained.
The archived-data/parser-review caveat limits confidence in the inputs. I have not followed any links or verified sources.
The main title appears twice consecutively in the Markdown.
No evidence of bond-market stress, ratings pressure or political deadlock is supplied; the explicit crisis caveat makes that limitation clear.
